BEGINNER1. What is an Array?

An array is an ordered, zero-indexed list of values. Arrays are actually objects under the hood, and can hold a mix of any type — numbers, strings, objects, even other arrays.

Real-world analogy: An array is like a numbered parking lot. Each spot has a fixed number starting at 0. You can park at the end, remove from the end, or use a bulldozer (splice) to change the middle. 
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
console.log(fruits[0]);      // "apple" — first element, index 0
console.log(fruits.length);  // 3

const mixed = [1, "two", true, { id: 4 }, [5, 6]]; // any types allowed

BEGINNER2. Creating & Accessing Arrays

// Literal — the common way
const arr = [1, 2, 3];

// Constructor — rarely used, has a quirky single-number case
const arr2 = new Array(1, 2, 3);   // [1, 2, 3]
const arr3 = new Array(3);         // [ <3 empty items> ] — NOT [3]! length 3, no values

// Access
arr[0];                 // first element
arr[arr.length - 1];    // last element — 3
arr[10];                // undefined — out of range, no error

// Checking type
Array.isArray(arr);     // true
typeof arr;             // "object" — NOT "array"!
⚠️ Common Pitfall: new Array(3) creates an EMPTY array with length 3, not an array containing the number 3. Always prefer the array literal syntax [3] or [1,2,3] to avoid this trap entirely.

BEGINNER3. Mutating Methods

These methods CHANGE the original array in place.

const a = [1, 2, 3];

a.push(4);       // a → [1,2,3,4]   returns 4 (new length)
a.pop();         // a → [1,2,3]     returns 4 (the removed element)
a.unshift(0);    // a → [0,1,2,3]   returns 4 (new length)
a.shift();       // a → [1,2,3]     returns 0 (the removed element)
a.splice(1, 1);  // a → [1,3]       returns [2] (removed elements)
a.splice(1, 0, 5, 6); // a → [1,5,6,3] — insert without removing (deleteCount = 0)

a.reverse();     // reverses in place
a.sort();        // sorts in place (see Section 8 for the gotcha!)
a.fill(0);       // replaces every element with 0
Method Effect Returns
push(v)Add to endNew length
pop()Remove from endRemoved element
unshift(v)Add to frontNew length
shift()Remove from frontRemoved element
splice(start,count,...items)Remove/insert anywhereArray of removed items

BEGINNER4. Non-Mutating Methods

These methods return a NEW array or value, leaving the original untouched.

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];

nums.slice(1, 3);              // [2, 3] — copy of a portion (end index excluded)
nums.map(x => x * 2);          // [2, 4, 6, 8] — transform every element
nums.filter(x => x % 2 === 0); // [2, 4] — keep elements matching a test
nums.concat([5, 6]);           // [1,2,3,4,5,6] — merge arrays
nums.join("-");                // "1-2-3-4" — turn into a string
nums.flat();                   // flattens one level of nested arrays

console.log(nums); // [1, 2, 3, 4] — completely unchanged!

flatMap — map() + flat() Combined

const sentences = ["hello world", "foo bar"];
sentences.flatMap(s => s.split(" "));
// ["hello", "world", "foo", "bar"] — split then flattened in one step

INTERMEDIATE5. Searching & Testing

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

nums.find(x => x > 3);         // 4 — first match, or undefined if none
nums.findIndex(x => x > 3);    // 3 — index of first match, or -1
nums.findLast(x => x > 3);     // 5 — last match, searching from the end
nums.includes(3);              // true
nums.indexOf(3);               // 2 — index, or -1 if not found
nums.some(x => x > 4);         // true — at least one matches
nums.every(x => x > 0);        // true — ALL elements match
⚠️ Common Pitfall: indexOf returns 0 for the first element, which is FALSY — writing if (arr.indexOf(x)) is a bug because index 0 is treated as "not found." Always check !== -1, or use includes() for a plain boolean answer. 
const arr = ["a", "b", "c"];
if (arr.indexOf("a")) { }        // ❌ bug — indexOf returns 0, which is falsy!
if (arr.indexOf("a") !== -1) { } // ✅ correct
if (arr.includes("a")) { }       // ✅ clearest — includes() returns a real boolean

ADVANCED6. reduce() Deep Dive

reduce() "folds" an array down into a single value — a sum, an object, another array, anything. It's the most flexible (and most confusing at first) array method.

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];

// Sum — accumulator starts at 0
const total = nums.reduce((acc, cur) => acc + cur, 0);
console.log(total); // 10

// Building an object — counting occurrences
const votes = ["yes", "no", "yes", "yes", "no"];
const tally = votes.reduce((acc, vote) => {
    acc[vote] = (acc[vote] || 0) + 1;
    return acc;
}, {});
console.log(tally); // { yes: 3, no: 2 }

// Flattening nested arrays
const nested = [[1,2], [3,4], [5]];
const flat = nested.reduce((acc, arr) => acc.concat(arr), []);
console.log(flat); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
💡 Tip: Always pass the initial value (the second argument to reduce) explicitly. If you omit it, reduce uses the array's first element as the starting accumulator — which breaks on an empty array (TypeError) and can produce confusing results.

INTERMEDIATE7. Spread & Destructuring

Spread — Copy and Merge

const a = [1, 2], b = [3, 4];
const merged = [...a, ...b];   // [1, 2, 3, 4]
const copy = [...a];           // [1, 2] — shallow copy, new array

// Spread also works to pass array elements as separate function arguments
console.log(Math.max(...[3, 7, 1])); // 7

Destructuring

const [first, second, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
console.log(first, second, rest); // 10  20  [30, 40]

// Skipping elements
const [, , third] = ["a", "b", "c"];
console.log(third); // "c"

// Default values during destructuring
const [x = 1, y = 2] = [undefined, 99];
console.log(x, y); // 1  99 (x used its default, y kept its actual value)
⚠️ Shallow Copy Only: [...arr] copies the TOP-LEVEL elements. If those elements are themselves objects/arrays, both the original and the copy still point to the SAME nested objects. 
const original = [{ id: 1 }];
const shallow = [...original];
shallow[0].id = 99;
console.log(original[0].id); // 99 — the nested object is shared!

ADVANCED8. Sorting Correctly

sort() WITHOUT a comparator converts every element to a STRING and sorts lexicographically — which produces wrong results for numbers.

const nums = [10, 1, 21, 2];
nums.sort();
console.log(nums); // [1, 10, 2, 21] — WRONG for numeric order! ("10" < "2" as strings)

// ✅ Provide a comparator function
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b); // ascending
console.log(nums); // [1, 2, 10, 21]

nums.sort((a, b) => b - a); // descending
console.log(nums); // [21, 10, 2, 1]

Sorting Objects

const people = [{ name: "Bob", age: 25 }, { name: "Alice", age: 30 }];
people.sort((a, b) => a.age - b.age);       // ascending by age
people.sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); // alphabetical, locale-aware
💡 Tip: Modern JavaScript engines guarantee sort() is stable — elements that compare equal keep their original relative order. This matters when sorting by multiple criteria in sequence.

ADVANCED9. Common Pitfalls

1. sort() Mutates the Original Array

const original = [3, 1, 2];
const sorted = original.sort();
console.log(original === sorted); // true — same array, sort() mutates AND returns it!

// ✅ To sort without mutating, copy first
const safelySorted = [...original].sort();

2. forEach Cannot Be Broken Out Of

[1, 2, 3].forEach(n => {
    if (n === 2) return; // ⚠️ only skips THIS iteration, does NOT stop the loop
    console.log(n);
});
// Output: 1  3  — for a real early exit, use a plain for/for...of loop instead

3. forEach Always Returns undefined

const result = [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => n * 2);
console.log(result); // undefined — forEach never collects return values, use map() instead

4. Sparse Arrays / Holes

const sparse = [1, , 3]; // a "hole" at index 1
console.log(sparse.length);      // 3
console.log(sparse[1]);          // undefined
sparse.forEach(x => console.log(x)); // 1, 3 — forEach SKIPS holes entirely!

INTERMEDIATE10. Best Practices

1. Prefer Non-Mutating Methods for Predictable Code

// ✅ Original data stays intact — easier to reason about and debug
const updated = items.map(item => item.id === id ? { ...item, done: true } : item);

// ❌ Mutating shared state can cause hard-to-trace bugs
items.find(item => item.id === id).done = true;

2. Always Provide a Sort Comparator for Numbers

// ✅ Correct numeric sort
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);

// ❌ Lexicographic (string) sort — wrong for numbers
nums.sort();

3. Use Array.isArray(), Not typeof, to Detect Arrays

Array.isArray(value); // ✅ reliable
typeof value === "object"; // ❌ true for arrays too — doesn't distinguish them

4. Use includes() for Boolean Membership Checks

// ✅ Clear and correct
if (arr.includes(target)) { }

// ❌ Fragile — indexOf(0) is falsy!
if (arr.indexOf(target)) { }

5. Give reduce() an Explicit Initial Value

// ✅ Safe even on an empty array
arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0);

// ❌ Throws on empty arrays, and starting value is implicit
arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x);

📋 Quick Reference Summary

Concept Key Points
Mutating push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill — change the original.
Non-mutating slice, map, filter, concat, flat, join — return a new array/value.
Searching find, findIndex, includes, indexOf, some, every.
reduce Folds an array into a single value — always pass an initial value.
Spread/Destructure [...arr] shallow-copies; [a, b, ...rest] = arr unpacks.
sort() Mutates in place; without a comparator, sorts as strings — always pass (a,b) => a-b for numbers.

Intermediate: Understand sections 5, 7, 10
